answers.solution:
Title: The Origin and Practice of Yoga

Yoga began in ancient India thousands of years ago, even before any religion. Shiva, believed to be the first yogi and guru, passed his knowledge to seven sages, who carried it to many parts of the world, though India kept it in its fullest form. Remains of the Indus-Saraswati civilisation, folk traditions and Buddhist and Jain traditions show that yoga was practised in ancient India under a guru, with great stress on its spiritual value. Sun worship in the Vedic age later gave rise to Suryanamaskar. Maharishi Patanjali, the father of modern yoga, did not invent it but arranged its many forms into one system, the Yoga Sutras. Breath is central to yoga: asanas are done with slow movements and smooth, relaxed breathing.

Topics attempted: (a) and (b).

(a) The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins with a Single Step

This famous saying of the Chinese thinker Lao Tzu teaches us that every great achievement starts with a small beginning. A long journey seems frightening when we think of the whole distance, but it becomes possible once we take the first step and keep walking.

Many people dream of big goals but never start, because the task looks too big. A student who wants to top the class must begin by learning one chapter well today. An athlete who wants to win a medal must start with a short run each morning.

Small, steady steps add up to great results. Gandhiji's Dandi March began with a handful of followers and grew into a mighty movement. So we should not wait for the perfect moment. We should begin today, however small the step.

(b) Need to Educate the Girl Child

Education is the right of every child, yet in many parts of our country girls are still kept at home while their brothers go to school. This must change, because educating a girl means educating a whole family.

An educated girl grows into a confident woman who can earn her own living and stand on her own feet. She takes better care of her family's health and nutrition, and she makes sure her own children go to school. Education also protects girls from child marriage and teaches them their rights.

The government has started schemes such as 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao', but schemes alone are not enough. Parents and society must change their thinking. When every girl is educated, our nation will truly progress.

A Costly Friendship

Ravi was travelling by train to Delhi with a briefcase full of money for his sister's wedding. A well-dressed man sitting beside him was very friendly. He shared his food and told funny stories, and soon Ravi trusted him completely.

At a big station the train stopped for fifteen minutes. Ravi felt hungry and decided to buy some snacks. 'Don't worry, I'll look after your bag,' said his new friend with a smile.

When Ravi returned, both the man and the briefcase were gone. Ravi was shocked and burst into tears. He reported the theft to the railway police, but the thief was never found. Ravi had learnt a bitter lesson: never trust a stranger too quickly.

answers.label: Q6
answers.solution:
Topics attempted: (a) and (c).

(a) Failures Are the Stepping Stones to Success

Nobody likes to fail, but failure is not the end of the road. In fact, it is often the first step towards success. Each failure shows us our mistakes and teaches us what to do better next time.

Thomas Edison tried hundreds of materials before he made a working electric bulb. He said he had not failed, but had only found many ways that did not work. Abraham Lincoln lost many elections before he became President of America.

What matters is how we respond to failure. If we lose heart and give up, failure defeats us. If we learn from it and try again with greater effort, it becomes a stepping stone. So we should never be afraid of failing, because every fall teaches us how to rise higher.

(c) Time and Tide Wait for None

This proverb reminds us that time keeps moving and never stops for anyone, just as the tide of the sea comes and goes at its fixed hour. Once time is lost, it can never be brought back.

A student who wastes his days in play and idle talk repents when the examinations come near. A farmer who does not sow his seeds in the right season gets no harvest. A soldier who delays even for a moment on the battlefield may lose his life.

Successful people value every minute. They plan their work, keep to a timetable and never put off today's work till tomorrow. We too should use our time wisely, because money lost can be earned again, but time lost is lost forever.

12 June 2018

The Editor
The Times of India
New Delhi

Subject: Students distracted from their studies by Facebook and WhatsApp

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to express my concern about how social media apps like Facebook and WhatsApp are distracting students from their studies.

Today almost every student has a smartphone. Many spend hours chatting, sharing photographs and watching videos on these apps. A student sits down to study, but every few minutes a message arrives and breaks his attention. Many stay up late at night on their phones and come to school tired. As a result, their concentration, their marks and even their health are suffering.

These apps are not bad in themselves; they can be used to share notes and keep in touch with friends. The problem is overuse. Parents should fix screen time for their children, and schools should teach students to use social media wisely. Students themselves must show self-control and keep their phones away while studying.

I hope this letter will make students and parents think seriously about the problem.

Yours faithfully,
XYZ

The Need for Sanitation

Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and my dear friends.

Today I wish to speak on a subject that touches all our lives: the need for sanitation.

When we walk through our town, we see heaps of garbage by the roadside, open drains, overflowing dustbins, and people spitting and littering everywhere. These insanitary conditions are not just ugly; they are dangerous. Flies and mosquitoes breed in dirt and spread diseases like malaria, dengue, cholera and typhoid. Dirty water causes stomach infections, and the foul smell makes life unpleasant for everyone.

Good sanitation means clean surroundings, safe drinking water, proper toilets and the correct disposal of waste. It is the first step towards good health. Gandhiji said that cleanliness is next to godliness, and the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan reminds us of the same.

The municipality must do its part, but we too have a duty. Let us use dustbins, separate wet and dry waste, keep our drains clear and never litter. Let us also persuade our families and neighbours to do the same.

A clean town is a healthy town. Let us begin today.

Thank you.
